title: Crew backlog
subtitle: Shared, ordered, and reviewed in the repo. Drag to rank; approve what we should do next.

items.title: Confirm whether 0.7.7 actually stopped the jitter
items.detail: 0.7.7 makes the calm working animation the default, which is the leading explanation for sessions jittering up and down: the mascot ran an independently phased 1.5s bob-and-scale per working session. Installing 0.7.7 is the experiment. Everything else in this group is conditional on the answer, so it is ranked first.
items.why: Two candidate fixes shipped and neither is confirmed against the real symptom. Until this is answered we are guessing.
items.evidence: PR #38; migration 2026-10-calm-motion-default

items.title: Check whether the font-load re-fit ever re-measures the cell
items.detail: CrewTerminal runs document.fonts.ready.then(fit), but fit() only re-proposes dimensions; xterm recomputes character size on charSizeChanged, which a plain fit does not raise. If a pane opened before JetBrains Mono finished loading keeps the fallback metrics, it stays on Menlo's device.cell.height of 35 - odd, and therefore inside the oscillating regime that PR #39 addresses.
items.why: This is the most plausible remaining mechanism for a pane to sit permanently in the unstable regime, and it is the likeliest third cause if CB-1 comes back negative.
items.evidence: Measured: JetBrains Mono -> 40 (even, stable); Menlo/ui-monospace -> 35 (odd, unstable) at dpr 2

items.title: Measure cell metrics in the running app, not a harness
items.detail: The numbers behind PR #39 came from headless Chromium mirroring xterm's arithmetic. Log term._core._renderService.dimensions.device.cell.height and window.devicePixelRatio from a live pane instead, so the scope claim rests on the real app rather than a reconstruction.
items.why: The harness and xterm's CharSizeService could diverge in font fallback or measurement API. One log line retires the doubt permanently.
items.evidence: test/e2e/flicker-probe.mjs already attaches over CDP

items.title: De-duplicate the two terminal fit loops
items.detail: src/renderer/terminal/xterm-engine.ts and src/renderer/components/TerminalView.tsx carry byte-identical copies of the 3-pass fit loop and its 15-line comment. Extract one implementation both call.
items.why: This already bit us: a fix written against the engine copy left TerminalView untouched, and TerminalView is the path users are on unless they opted into the enhanced terminal. Two copies means every terminal fix is half a fix.
items.evidence: xterm-engine.ts:417-437 and TerminalView.tsx:120-140; flagged in code review of PR #39

items.title: Correct or remove the fit loop's scrollbar rationale
items.detail: The comment says the loop iterates because FitAddon subtracts a viewport scrollbar whose existence depends on the proposed size. But xterm assigns Viewport.scrollBarWidth once, in the constructor, and never re-measures it - so that rationale cannot operate within a single synchronous call. Either the loop converges for a different reason (DOM-renderer rounding, worth +/-1 column) or it does not need three passes.
items.why: A confidently wrong comment is worse than none: it is why the loop survived scrutiny this long, and it misled a fix earlier today.
items.evidence: node_modules/@xterm/xterm/src/browser/Viewport.ts:70, single assignment

items.title: Make the resize/report asymmetry structurally impossible
items.detail: fit() can call term.resize() on an early pass and then return null on a later one, which would leave the grid resized while the PTY keeps its old width. It was proven unreachable today - the mount cannot collapse mid-loop, cell dimensions never fall to zero, and the proposal moves by at most one column - so this is hardening, not a bug fix.
items.why: It is latent rather than live. Worth doing when CB-4 extracts the loop anyway, and not worth a standalone change: a fix was written for it today and correctly reverted as dead code.
items.evidence: Reverted branch fix/fit-pty-sync; review concluded unreachable

items.title: Get the e2e gate running again
items.detail: RELEASING.md lists test/e2e as a release prerequisite, but it cannot run on this Mac: the Electron supplied by the corporate npm proxy is refused by Gatekeeper ('notarization indicates this code has been revoked') and MDM blocks re-signing it in place. Either run the suite on a macOS CI runner, or point the harness at the signed packaged app via Playwright's executablePath.
items.why: 0.7.6 and 0.7.7 both shipped without it. A gate nobody can run is not a gate, and right now only unit tests and a PTY smoke test stand between a regression and a release.
items.evidence: spctl -a -vv on node_modules/electron/dist/Electron.app; codesign returns 'Operation not permitted'

items.title: Stabilise the flaky release-script tests
items.detail: test/release-scripts.test.ts shells out to bash and intermittently fails under full-suite parallelism - two failures in one run, then 34/34 green in isolation and on re-run. Give them deterministic timeouts or isolate them from the parallel pool.
items.why: A suite that fails randomly at release time trains us to re-run until green, which is exactly how a real failure gets waved through.
items.evidence: Observed during the 0.7.7 release run

items.title: Script the worktree node_modules dance
items.detail: Every worktree holds a git-tracked node_modules symlink pointing at an empty target, so tests and builds fail until it is repointed at a worktree that has a real install - and the Electron binary inside it gets removed periodically, which then fails with an opaque ENOENT. Wrap setup and restore in one script.
items.why: It cost several detours in this session alone, and each one looks like a code failure before it turns out to be the environment.
items.evidence: Hit three times today: empty target, missing Electron.app, dirty tree blocking publish.sh

items.title: Decide whether the lively mascot animation stays at all
items.detail: 0.7.7 flips the default to calm and migrates existing installs once. If nobody turns the lively animation back on, the second code path, its CSS, and the per-session will-change compositor layer can go.
items.why: Keeping both costs a settings row, a migration, a test fixture that must start from the lively state, and a compositor layer per working session.
items.size: An hour, after a few weeks of use
items.evidence: test/renderer-regressions.test.ts:639-660 depends on the lively default

items.title: Sign the Windows build
items.detail: Windows artifacts ship unsigned and raise a SmartScreen warning on first run, as RELEASING.md notes.
items.why: It is the roughest edge a new Windows user meets, before they have any reason to trust the app.
items.evidence: RELEASING.md, opening paragraph

items.title: Implement Conductor phase 1c
items.detail: Carried as known-and-accepted through several sessions. Worth either scheduling or explicitly closing, rather than continuing to carry it.
items.why: Long-lived unscheduled work quietly becomes a commitment nobody revisits. Ranking it here forces the choice.
items.evidence: Conductor spec, phase 1c

items.title: Give a session a working directory when you create it
items.detail: All 131 sessions in the store have cwd = $HOME, and recentDirs is empty — the directory picker has never been used once. Every agent therefore starts in home and has to be told where the work is, in prose, every single time. Capture a project directory at creation: default to the last directory used for that label, offer recent/starred repos, and infer from the label when it matches a known checkout. Populate recentDirs so the second session in a project is a one-click affair.
items.why: This is the clearest gap the data shows, and it is invisible in the UI: nothing signals that cwd is a thing you were meant to set. Every session pays a prompt-tax to explain where it is.
items.evidence: crew-store.json: 131/131 sessions cwd=/Users/alexselig; recentDirs: []

items.title: Make restore selective instead of all-or-nothing
items.detail: 98 of 131 sessions arrived in two programmatic bursts (2026-08-19 and 2026-08-26) with median gaps between creations of 0.75s and 0.14s — machine speed, not human. Of the 66 restored on 26 Aug, 54 were never prompted again; of the 32 on 19 Aug, all 32 were never prompted. Restore faithfully rebuilds everything and you then use almost none of it. Offer a restore preview: which sessions, last actually used when, select a subset. Default the selection to sessions with a real prompt in the last N days.
items.why: Restore is the single biggest source of clutter in the store, and the clutter is what makes every later list, view and grouping feature necessary.
items.evidence: Creation-gap analysis of crew-store.json; the 36-session set literally named 'Recovered'

items.title: Add a real archive, because the store is already 90% archive
items.detail: 117 of 131 sessions are past the 72-hour staleHideHours cutoff; only 14 are visible. The other 103 are not gone, they are hidden — still loaded, still restored, still in every file write. Hiding was the cheap version of a lifecycle. Add an explicit archive state with its own view, a restore-from-archive path, and a real delete. Then stop loading archived sessions into the live roster at all.
items.why: The store grows forever and has no exit. Hiding masks the symptom while the cost (load, persist, restore) keeps compounding.
items.evidence: crew-store.json: 117/131 older than staleHideHours=72; sessions[] has no archived/deleted state

items.title: Treat standing projects and scratch sessions as different things
items.detail: Of the 40 sessions ever actually prompted, the split is bimodal: 14 standing projects with a median 27-day life (Crew, Eval Atlas, Portfolio, Work Website, FDE, Groundtruth Mapper, the skill sessions) and 17 same-day throwaways (spec cleanup, Vertical Blog, Rounded Corners Spec). The app treats both identically — same persistence, same restore, same roster weight. Let a session be promoted to a standing project (always restored, always visible, pinned) or marked scratch (never restored, auto-archived at end of day).
items.why: One lifecycle for two species is why the roster needs so much hiding and grouping machinery. Sort it at the source.
items.evidence: Lifespan analysis of the 40 prompted sessions: 14 over 7 days, 17 under 1 day

items.title: Offer to resume prior work instead of silently creating a duplicate
items.detail: 24 sessions share a duplicated label — 'Develop Week In Review App', 'Create Project Tracker Site', 'Fix Icon Positioning Bug' and nine others each exist twice. That is the same job started again, with the earlier session's context stranded. On creation, when a label (or directory) matches an existing session, offer Resume that one as the primary action and Create a new one as the secondary.
items.why: Duplicates are how context gets lost: the work continues but the thread doesn't. The data shows it happening roughly one time in five.
items.evidence: crew-store.json: 12 labels occurring twice, covering 24 of 131 sessions

items.title: Lean on tags, which you use, rather than workspaces, which you mostly do not
items.detail: Tags are on 86 of 131 sessions (WORK 24, TOOLS 17, Other 12, FDE 9, Game 8, CREW 7, craft 5, SKILLS 4). Workspaces are assigned on only 43, leaving 88 unassigned, and two of the four workspaces are near-empty (HACK 6, OCTOBER 7). You adopted the lightweight primitive and skipped the heavyweight one. Make tags first-class: filter and group by tag, a saved view per tag, tag colours in the roster — and consider deriving workspaces from tags rather than maintaining both.
items.why: Two overlapping grouping systems, one adopted twice as much as the other. Invest in the one that won.
items.evidence: crew-store.json: tag set on 86/131; workspaceIds empty on 88/131

items.title: Decide whether custom agents earn their place
items.detail: All four agents in the store are the seeded builtins (UX Critique, Code Review, Security Review, Doc Writer) and not one custom agent has ever been created. There is exactly one custom view, 'Core Focus'. Either the authoring path is undiscoverable or the need is already met by the four defaults. Before building more agent surface, find out which — then either make authoring reachable from where agents are used, or freeze the feature at four good builtins and spend the room elsewhere.
items.why: This is a build-versus-cut decision, and right now it would be made on vibes. It is also the clearest thing the proposed opt-in tracking would settle.
items.evidence: crew-store.json: agents[] all builtin:true; customViews[] length 1

items.title: Add opt-in, local-only usage insights
items.detail: Flat off by default, with a plain-language consent screen that says exactly what is recorded, and nothing leaves the machine — append-only JSONL in Application Support, viewable in-app, with a one-click wipe. There is no third-party analytics in Crew today and none should be added. Record counters and durations, never prompt or terminal content: session opened/focused/closed, prompts per session, foreground dwell time, which view (grid, focus, custom) is used, agent and conductor invocations, restore accepted versus dismissed, crashes and PTY failures. Ship a 'Your usage' panel that shows you your own numbers, so the feature pays the user back rather than only paying us.
items.why: The analysis behind CB-13 to CB-19 had to be reverse-engineered from two timestamps per session, and several questions were simply unanswerable: how long you actually work in a session, how many prompts it takes, which views you use, whether a session ended satisfied or abandoned. The memory census that exists ran on exactly one day (26 Aug) and the crash log has recorded 19 clean quits and zero crashes, so what instrumentation there is tells us almost nothing about use.
items.evidence: No analytics dependency anywhere in src/; crew-crash.log: 1289 memcensus samples all on 2026-08-26, 19 quits, 0 crashes

items.title: Stop treating memory and stability as the next performance problem
items.detail: The census recorded a JS heap of 15-28 MB against a 3586 MB limit, peak DOM 1681 nodes, and the crash log holds 19 clean quits with zero crashes across five weeks. Whatever is worth fixing next, it is not footprint or stability. Record this as a deliberate negative result so the next perf instinct gets checked against it, and re-measure only with a census that runs on more than one day and more than one tile.
items.why: Perf work is the easiest thing to start and the hardest to justify. The only measurement available says there is nothing here.
items.evidence: crew-crash.log: heapMB 15-28 of heapLimitMB 3586; 0 crashes, 19 quits, Aug 26 - Oct 3
